To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the frequency and strength of cyclones and associated wind patterns have decreased (increased) over the western Mediterranean and the eastern part of the North Atlantic (the western part of the North and Baltic Seas), particularly during winter.

cyclone frequency and surface wind velocity have been decreasing (increasing) in the western (northern) Mediterranean, and that these changes are partially responsible for the significant height of wave trends in the Atlantic.

cyclone frequency and surface wind magnitude trends in the North Atlantic sector have been significant and have led to a decrease of precipitation in southern and eastern Europe, while increasing precipitation and significant wave height in the northern and western regions of Europe.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the detection of the main changes in cyclones and surface winds over the Euro–Atlantic region and with the analysis of the link between these changes and changes in precipitation and significant wave height.
the detection of changes in wind and cyclone patterns over the Euro–Atlantic region and their impact on European precipitation and significant wave height trends.

the analysis of trends in the frequency of cyclone and the surface wind magnitude in the Euro–Atlantic region, the assessment of trends in significant wave heights in the North Atlantic, and the link between these trends and the European precipitation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in the Euro–Atlantic region, cyclone frequency and wind speed trends are responsible for the observed significant wave height trends in the Atlantic and for the precipitation trends in Europe.

the observed changes in cyclone frequency are related to changes in the large‐scale atmospheric patterns, which are responsible for the observed changes in precipitation and waves in the North Atlantic.
the observed changes in cyclone frequencies and surface wind magnitude are consistent with the observed changes in precipitation and significant wave height.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the observed trends in the frequency of cyclone activity and surface winds are consistent with trends in the frequency and magnitude of extreme wave heights, and that these changes are related to the phases of the main atmospheric circulation modes.
the changes observed in European precipitation are related, in large part, to changes in the frequency and intensity of low‐pressure systems.
cyclone and surface wind trends in the Euro‐Atlantic sector are related with the preferred phases and trends of major atmospheric patterns.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the trends in cyclone activity and surface wind magnitude, particularly for January–March, are well matched by corresponding trends in significant height of waves in the North Atlantic, and that these trends are related to the preferred phases of the major atmospheric circulation patterns.

the trends in cyclone frequency and wind magnitude, which are linked to the large‐scale atmospheric patterns, are responsible, at least in part, for the observed trends in precipitation and waves in the Euro‐Atlantic sector.

the observed trends in the frequency and intensity of low‐pressure systems and surface wind magnitude in the Euro–Atlantic domain are likely responsible for the trends in European precipitation and significant wave height in the Atlantic.
